# Volume 1 — CHAPTER XXVI. The Story Club Is Formed

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

JUNIOR Brierley struggled to return to a boring routine. Nell, especially, felt that life was dreadfully dull, tedious, and pointless following the cup of thrills she had been enjoying for weeks. Was it possible for her to return to the previous peaceful pastimes of that distant time preceding the concert? Initially, she confessed to Isolde that she truly doubted she was able to.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0000 }

“Isolde, I am absolutely sure that life will never be completely identical to how it used to be in those bygone times,” she uttered sorrowfully, as though she were speaking of an era that occurred a minimum of half a century ago. “Maybe I will become accustomed to it given time, yet I fear that everyday life is ruined for people by concerts. I imagine Thirza disliking them stems from that. Such a practical woman, Thirza is. Being practical must be significantly superior; even so, I do not think I would truly desire to become a practical individual, since they lack romance to such a degree. According to Mrs. Sowerby, I am in no peril of becoming one, though it is impossible to be sure. At this moment, my feeling is that I might still mature into a practical person. However, that could be solely due to my exhaustion. Last night, sleep eluded me for a remarkably long time. I merely remained awake, envisioning the concert repeatedly. That is a wonderful aspect of such events—recalling them brings so much joy.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0001 }

In the end, nevertheless, Brierley school drifted back to its former routine and resumed its former concerns. Of course, the concert had lasting effects. Opal Pettigrew and Emma White, having argued about which of them had priority regarding their chairs on the platform, ceased sharing a desk, which destroyed a promising three-year friendship. Flossie Tulk and Julia Bell were not on “speaking” terms for three months, since Flossie Tulk had remarked to Bessie Duckett that Julia Bell’s bow upon standing up to recite reminded her of a chicken twitching its head, a comment Bessie passed on to Julia. Not one of the Motts would interact with the Bells, as the Bells had stated that the Motts were assigned too large a share of the program, to which the Motts had replied that the Bells could not even correctly perform the small amount they were given. Lastly, Wilfred Mott engaged in a fight with Elias Purdy MacKinnon, owing to Elias Purdy’s statement that Nell Harcourt acted superior regarding her recitations, an encounter in which Elias Purdy was “licked”; as a result, Ella May, who was Elias Purdy’s sister, refused to “speak” to Nell Harcourt for the remainder of the winter. Aside from these small disagreements, the work within Miss Thorne’s tiny domain proceeded regularly and smoothly.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0002 }

The weeks of winter passed away. That winter proved uncommonly gentle, featuring such sparse snow that Isolde and Nell managed to travel the Aspen Path to school on almost a daily basis. They were stepping nimbly down the path on the day of Nell’s birthday, remaining watchful with their eyes and ears even as they talked continuously, since Miss Thorne had informed them that a paper titled “A Winter’s Walk in the Woods” would soon need to be written, making it necessary for them to pay attention.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0003 }

“Only consider, Isolde, today marks my thirteenth birthday,” Nell observed, her tone filled with wonder. “It is hard for me to grasp that my teen years have begun. Upon waking earlier today, I felt as though the entire world ought to have transformed. Having turned thirteen a month ago, you likely find it less of a new experience than I do. Life appears far more fascinating because of it. A pair of additional years will bring me to true adulthood. I find immense solace in knowing that when that time comes, people will no longer mock me for employing lengthy words.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0004 }

“Opal Pettigrew says that she intends to get a boyfriend the moment she turns fifteen,” Isolde said.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0005 }

“Opal Pettigrew has her mind on nothing except beaus,” Nell remarked with scorn. “She is secretly thrilled whenever someone posts her name on a take-notice, despite how angry she acts. However, I fear that remark was not very kind. Mrs. Wace tells us that we ought never to speak unkindly; yet those comments escape so frequently before one realizes, don't they? It is completely impossible for me to speak of Flossie Tulk without being unkind, which is why I avoid speaking of her entirely. You might have seen that. My goal is to emulate Mrs. Wace in every way I can, because I consider her faultless. Mr. Wace shares that opinion. According to Mrs. Sowerby, he adores the very soil under her feet, and she feels it isn't entirely proper for a clergyman to devote his heart so deeply to a earthly creature. Even so, Isolde, ministers are merely human and possess their own main weaknesses, the same as anyone else. Mrs. Wace and I had a most fascinating conversation regarding main weaknesses on the afternoon of last Sunday. There exist only a handful of subjects appropriate for Sunday conversation, and that topic is included. The main weakness I face is overindulging in imagination and neglecting my obligations. I am working extremely hard to master it, and since I have finally reached thirteen, maybe my progress will improve.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0006 }

“We will be allowed to put our hair up in four more years,” Isolde said. “Although Alice Bell wears hers up at only sixteen, I consider that ridiculous. My plan is to wait until my seventeenth year.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0007 }

“Were Alice Bell’s crooked nose mine,” Nell remarked with conviction, “I would not—well! I will refrain from finishing my thought since it was terribly unkind. Furthermore, I was measuring it against my own nose, which is vain. Ever since I was told that compliment regarding it a long time back, I fear my nose occupies my mind far too often. Indeed, it brings me immense solace. Oh, Isolde, see, a rabbit is over there. We must keep that in mind for our essay on the woods. It seems to me that the woods are every bit as enchanting during the winter as they are in the summer. Their stillness and whiteness make them appear to be resting and experiencing sweet dreams.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0008 }

“Writing that composition will not bother me once the moment arrives,” Isolde uttered with a sigh. “Describing the woods is something I can handle, yet Monday’s required assignment is awful. Imagine Miss Thorne instructing us to invent a story entirely from our own imaginations!”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0009 }

“Indeed, it is as simple as a blink,” Nell remarked.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0010 }

“Because you possess an imagination, it is simple for you,” Isolde fired back, “yet how would you manage if you had come into the world devoid of one? You have finished your composition already, I assume?”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0011 }

Nell gave a nod, attempting with great effort not to appear self-righteously pleased with herself, yet failing utterly.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0012 }

“I composed it this past Monday night. Its title is ‘The Jealous Rival; or In Death Not Divided.’ I recited it to Thirza, who declared it to be utter rubbish. Afterward, I recited it to Obed, and he remarked that it was splendid. That represents the type of reviewer I prefer. It is a sorrowful, tender tale. I simply wept like a baby as I wrote it. It concerns two lovely maidens named Lucinda Montmorency and Seraphine Seymour who resided in the same settlement and were deeply devoted to one another. Lucinda was a stately brunette boasting a crown of raven hair and smoldering dark eyes. Seraphine was a majestic blonde possessing hair resembling spun gold and soft violet eyes.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0013 }

“Nobody I ever saw had purple eyes,” Isolde said with doubt.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0014 }

“Nor did I. They were merely a product of my imagination. My desire was for something extraordinary. An alabaster brow belonged to Seraphine as well. The definition of an alabaster brow has now become clear to me. One benefit of attaining thirteen years of age is that. Your knowledge is considerably greater than it was at merely twelve.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0015 }

“Well, what happened to Lucinda and Seraphine?” inquired Isolde, whose curiosity regarding their destiny was starting to grow.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0016 }

“Until reaching sixteen years of age, their beauty developed side by side. At that point, Bertram DeVere arrived in their home village, falling deeply in love with the blonde Seraphine. His rescue of her occurred when her carriage horse bolted, leaving her unconscious in his arms as he transported her three miles back home, owing, as you can see, to the vehicle being completely destroyed. Visualizing the proposal proved quite difficult for me, given my total lack of personal experience. Consequently, I inquired of Opal Pettigrew whether she possessed any knowledge regarding how men pop the question, figuring she would be a reliable source since numerous sisters of hers were married. Opal revealed that she was concealed inside the hallway pantry when her sister Tabitha received a proposal from Malcolm Andres. According to her, Malcolm mentioned to Tabitha that his father had transferred the farm into his personal name, following up with, ‘What do you say, darling pet, if we get hitched this fall?’ To this, Tabitha replied, ‘Yes—no—I don’t know—let me see’—and just like that, their engagement was settled. However, judging that variety of proposal to lack true romance, I ultimately had to construct the scene from my own imagination as best I could. I crafted it to be extremely ornate and poetic, having Bertram drop to his knees, even though Opal Pettigrew claims that is no longer the custom. Seraphine gave her consent through a speech spanning an entire page. You can be sure I expended a great deal of effort on that monologue. After rewriting it five separate times, I regard it as my greatest work. Bertram presented her with a ruby necklace alongside a diamond ring and mentioned a honeymoon trip to Europe, being fabulously rich. Sadly, however, darkness soon commenced falling across their journey. Lucinda was privately harboring feelings for Bertram herself, and upon hearing Seraphine describe the engagement, she became absolutely enraged, particularly when viewing the diamond ring and the necklace. Every bit of her love for Seraphine transformed into intense hatred, leading her to swear that Bertram would never become her sister's husband. Nevertheless, she feigned being Seraphine’s friend just as before. One night, while they stood together on a bridge spanning a fast, violent river, Lucinda—believing no witnesses were present—shoved Seraphine over the edge, uttering a frantic, sneering, ‘Ha, ha, ha.’ Yet Bertram observed the entire event and immediately leaped into the rushing water, crying out, ‘I will save thee, my peerless Seraphine.’ Unfortunately, he had overlooked his inability to swim, resulting in both of them drowning while locked in a mutual embrace. Shortly thereafter, the water washed their corpses to the bank. They were laid to rest within a single grave during an exceedingly grand funeral service, Isolde. Concluding a tale with a burial is vastly more romantic than ending it with a marriage. Regarding Lucinda, guilt drove her completely mad, causing her to be locked away in an asylum. I viewed that outcome as a fittingly poetic punishment for her misdeed.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0017 }

“How completely wonderful!” breathed Isolde, whose critical style matched Obed’s. “It is beyond me how you create such exciting stories purely from your mind, Nell. I would love to have an imagination as strong as yours.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0018 }

“It would be if you’d only cultivate it,” Nell said cheeringly. “Isolde, I’ve just thought of a plan. Let’s have a story club that is just for you and me and write stories for practice. Until you can do them by yourself, I’ll help you along. You know, you ought to cultivate your imagination. Miss Thorne says so. We must take the right way, though. I told her about the Whispering Wood, but she said that in that, we went about it the wrong way.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0019 }

The tale-writing society originated in this manner. Its membership was restricted initially to Isolde and Nell, yet before long it broadened to embrace Odette Pullen, Opal Pettigrew, and a couple of additional people who believed their creative faculties required nurturing. Male members were strictly prohibited—even though Opal Pettigrew remarked that accepting them would heighten the thrill—and every single participant was required to generate a weekly tale.
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0020 }

“It is fascinating in the extreme,” Nell remarked to Thirza. “The girls must all present their tales by reading them aloud, after which a discussion takes place. Keeping every single one sacredly is our plan, so that future generations can read them. Every one of us uses a nom-de-plume when writing. Rosamond Montmorency is mine. Pretty well is how all the girls perform. Opal Pettigrew tends toward sentimentality. Too much romance gets included in her tales, and as you are aware, an excess is more undesirable than a shortage. None is ever included by Odette, for the reason that reading it out loud makes her feel exceedingly foolish, according to her. Extremely sensible describes the stories that Odette writes. Conversely, an overabundance of murders is placed into hers by Isolde. Her explanation is that killing the characters off to be rid of them is what she does because figuring out what else to do with them eludes her most of the time. Providing them with subjects to write about usually falls to me, yet having millions of ideas prevents that from being difficult.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0021 }

“I believe this tale-crafting affair is the most foolish thing so far,” Thirza mocked. “A bunch of absurdity will fill your minds, taking away hours that ought to be spent on your schoolwork. It is harmful enough to read stories, yet crafting them is even more detrimental.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0022 }

“Thirza, we take such care to include a moral in every single one,” Nell clarified. “That is something I require. Every good person receives a reward, and every bad person gets a proper punishment. Surely that produces a beneficial result. What matters most is the moral. Mr. Wace states this. When I recited a story of mine to him and Mrs. Wace, the two of them concurred that it possessed a wonderful moral. They simply laughed at inappropriate moments, though. My preference is for listeners to weep. Whenever I reach the sad sections, Odette and Opal nearly always shed tears. Isolde informed her Aunt Lavinia about the club in a letter, and in her reply, her Aunt Lavinia requested that we mail her a few of our tales. Consequently, we transcribed four of our absolute finest and dispatched them. Miss Lavinia Pembroke stated in her reply that she had not encountered anything so funny in all her days. That left us somewhat bewildered since those tales were entirely deeply sad, with nearly all the characters dying. Even so, I am pleased that Miss Pembroke enjoyed them. This demonstrates that our club accomplishes a bit of good on earth. According to Mrs. Wace, that should be what we aim for in all things. I truly endeavor to make that my aim, yet I slip up frequently whenever I am enjoying myself. My wish is to resemble Mrs. Wace slightly once I reach adulthood. Thirza, do you suppose there is any chance of that occurring?”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0023 }

“It doesn't seem to me that there was much” was the comforting reply from Thirza. “Mrs. Wace was certainly never the kind of foolish, absent-minded little girl that you are, I am certain.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0024 }

“No; yet she was not constantly as good as she is today either,” Nell said solemnly. “She disclosed it to me herself—meaning, she stated that she was a terrible mischief during her girlhood and was forever getting into trouble. I was so heartened when I learned that. Is it extremely sinful of me, Thirza, to be heartened when I learn that different folks have been evil and mischievous? Mrs. Sowerby claims it is. Mrs. Sowerby claims she constantly feels appalled when she learns of anybody ever having been bad, regardless of how young they were. Mrs. Sowerby claims she one time heard a clergyman admit that during his boyhood he took a strawberry tart from his aunt’s pantry and she never possessed any regard for that clergyman afterwards. Now, I would not have experienced it like that. I would have believed that it was truly grand of him to admit it, and I would have believed what a heartening matter it would be for young boys currently who perform bad deeds and feel remorseful for them to realize that maybe they might turn out to be clergymen regardless of it. That is how I would experience it, Thirza.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0025 }

“As I am currently feeling, Nell,” Thirza remarked, “you ought to have those dishes cleaned by now. All of your talking has made you take thirty minutes more than you ought to have. Master working before you speak.”
{: #nw-v01-c26-p0026 }
